Twist rate vs. bullet weight and velocity well understood by marksmen reloaders all the way back to the late 1800s. If you belong to a range find the old guy with bench setup & spotting scope shooting 5 rounds into dime sized groups. He'll tell you chapter & verse about it. Understanding the relationship and optimizing your load accordingly is the key to accuracy. There is a lot of data on the M16 that explains it in more detail but here is the short version. I got my first AR15 in the 80s when this discussion was boiling over. By that time many of the shortfalls of the original configuration were known. Mainly the lack of poor performance at long distance. What worked in Vietnam and close range was not so hot out in the desert, the next anticipated war zone.

The most common twist rate for the original M16 twist rate was 1:12 and optimized for a 55 gr. bullet. IIRC the round becomes deliberately unstable under ~100 yds. This was meant to get a larger wound from less than optimal shot placement. Whereas a heavier bullet would go straight through, the lighter one would yaw.. In doing so it created a a much larger channel.

In the early 80s the M16A2 came out with a 1:7 twist and optimized for a heavier bullet and much better at long distances. Bullet did not yaw and remained true so better for accuracy at extreme range. Can't recall who lead this change, likely the USMC. This change was only on rifle config M16s and not carbines which remained 1:12 and more inline with their near SMG role. If you look many/most AR15 barrelled uppers have 1:7 twist rates.

Finally, either before or after Gulf War 1 the 1:9 twist was introduced alongside the others. IIRC the 62gr. bullet works fine in it. Not sure if that is still a common twist outside of the military though and not sure if still issued. Kind of a moot point with with the new 6.8mm round going into service. Have not paid much attention though beyond 1:12 as that is what barrels are on my AR15s so 55gr. bullets only for them.

To be autistic about it you'll be working with:

Bullet weight

Bullet type

Barrel length

Barrel twist rate

Ideal target range

Not enough spin and its inaccurate. Too much and the bullet will fly apart.

Impact outside of ideal velocity range means the bullet may not expand, this is a bigger deal with hunting bullets.

Longer barrel = more faster but gun is more heavier and longer and can be awkward

Short barrel = lower velocity and fearsomely huge muzzle flash

It's all a tradeoff. Big magical super zooper rounds sound like theyd be great except when they're so hot they burn out your barrel in 300 shots.
